What is "System Data" and how do I reduce it?⟦0⟧

It's the catch-all category in Storage settings: caches, Time Machine local snapshots, app support data, logs, and virtual machine or Docker disks. Scan your disk with DiskGarden to see it folder by folder; our guide What is System Data on a Mac explains what's safe to remove.
How do I free up space on my Mac?⟦0⟧

Find the biggest folders first — scan with DiskGarden and follow the widest petals — then check the usual suspects: Downloads, old iPhone backups, Xcode and Docker data, caches and videos. The full walkthrough: How to free up space on your Mac.
Is it safe to empty the Waste bin?⟦0⟧

Yes, as long as you've looked over what's in it. DiskGarden only removes what you put there, shows each item's size and path first, and refuses to take system folders such as /System, /Library and /usr. On the map, press Space to Quick Look anything before you drop it in; in the Waste bin, right-click an item to show it in Finder or take it back out.
By default, emptying moves the items to the Trash, so you can still get them back from there.
Can I scan an external drive or a network share?⟦0⟧

Yes. Every volume your Mac has mounted — USB and Thunderbolt drives, SD cards, disk images, Time Machine disks and network shares — shows up on the Volumes page. Network shares scan more slowly, since every folder is read over the network.

DiskGarden User Guide — Scan, Read the Map, Free Up Space
How to use DiskGarden: scan a disk, read the map, clear space safely with the Waste bin, Deep Scan (Admin), external drives and keyboard shortcuts.
User guide
Everything DiskGarden does, from your first scan to emptying the Waste bin.
Also read: How to free up space on your Mac · What is System Data on a Mac?
Download DiskGarden from the Download page, open the .dmg and drag the app to Applications. The first time you open it, macOS asks whether to open an app downloaded from the internet — choose Open.
DiskGarden opens on the Volumes page: every mounted disk, with a ring showing how full it is and how much space is free. A ring turns orange, then red, as a disk runs low.
Your first scan
Click a disk (or its Scan button). The ring fills as DiskGarden reads the disk.
When it's done, the map opens. Next time the button says View: DiskGarden remembers the result between launches and keeps it up to date as files change.
To map a single folder instead, click Scan a folder…, press ⌘ O, or drop the folder onto the window.
The ▾ next to a disk's button has more: rescan, Deep Scan (Admin), clear the scan results.

The map is a bloom of rings around a center disc. The disc shows how much space is used. The first ring holds the top-level folders, the next ring their contents, and so on outward. Each petal is as wide as the space it takes, so the biggest things are the widest petals.

Colours group things that belong together: a folder's contents share its part of the colour wheel, getting lighter toward the edge. When you grow into a folder, its contents spread over the whole wheel again.
Grey "small items…" petals gather the files and folders too small to draw one by one.

Purple "hidden space…" is space the disk reports as used that the scan couldn't reach: other users' files, protected system folders, snapshots and purgeable space. A Deep Scan (Admin) maps most of it.
Moving around
Hover a petal to see its name, size and share of the disk; the list on the left highlights it too.
Click a folder petal to grow into it. Click the center disc, use the path at the top, or press ⌘ ↑ to come back out.
The list on the left shows the current folder's contents with their sizes. Below it, Available and Available (incl. purgeable) show how much room the disk has.
The Waste bin, at the bottom left of the map, is where you collect things to remove. Putting something in it deletes nothing.
Drop a petal or a row from the list onto the Waste bin, or hover it and press ⌘ ⌫.
Review. The Waste bin lists every item with its size and path. Right-click an item to show it in Finder or take it back out. Before dropping something in, press Space on the map to Quick Look it.
Empty when you're sure. By default the items move to the Trash, so you can still recover them there. If you turn off Emptying moves files to the Trash in Settings, they're deleted right away.
What can never go in the Waste bin
System locations — such as ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧ and the top level of your disk — are shown on the map so you can understand your disk, but DiskGarden won't let you put them in the Waste bin.
Some of your disk is off limits to normal apps: other users' home folders, parts of the system and some caches. That's where the purple hidden space comes from.
Choose Deep Scan (Admin) from the ▾ menu next to a disk and enter your Mac's password. DiskGarden scans again with administrator rights and maps what it couldn't see before.

For the most complete map, also give DiskGarden Full Disk Access: open System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access, and switch DiskGarden on. DiskGarden's own Settings has a Full Disk Access tab that tells you whether it's allowed.
Revoking access
Administrator rights last only for that one scan. To take back Full Disk Access, switch DiskGarden off (or remove it) in System Settings → Privacy & Security → Full Disk Access.

Anything your Mac mounts appears on the Volumes page automatically: USB and Thunderbolt drives, SD cards, disk images (.dmg), Time Machine disks and network shares (SMB, AFP, NFS, WebDAV). Plug in a drive and it appears; unplug it and it disappears.
Star a folder you scanned (the ★ next to its name) to keep it on the Volumes page for next time.
Network shares scan more slowly than local disks, since every folder is read over the network.
Time Machine backups are full of hard links; DiskGarden counts each file once, so the map shows the space the backup really uses.

DiskGarden Privacy Policy
What DiskGarden sends and what it never sends: your files and scans stay on your Mac.
Privacy
DiskGarden is built to look at your disk without looking at you. Here is exactly what goes online.
Your files stay on your Mac

Scanning happens entirely on your Mac. The map, the names and sizes of your files and folders, and your saved scan results are stored locally (in ⟦0⟧) and are never uploaded. DiskGarden has no account, no ads and no analytics.
What does go online
Update checks

A few times a day DiskGarden downloads a small list of available versions from diskgarden.app (using the open-source Sparkle framework), and downloads an update when there is one. Like any web request, this reveals your IP address and the app's version to the server.
Crash reports

If DiskGarden crashes or hits a serious error, it sends a report using Firebase Crashlytics (Google): the app and macOS versions, the Mac model, what the app was doing in code at the time, and the error message. An error message can occasionally include the path of the file or folder involved. Reports are tied to a random installation ID, not to you, and are used only to fix bugs.
Remote settings
DiskGarden fetches a few settings from Firebase Remote Config (Google), so features can be tuned or switched off without a new release. This request also uses the random installation ID.
Google's handling of this data is described in the Firebase privacy and security documentation.
This website
diskgarden.app uses no cookies, no analytics and no trackers. It is hosted on GitHub Pages, which may log visitors' IP addresses for security; see GitHub's privacy statement.

How to free up space on your Mac
"Your disk is almost full." Here's how to find out what is actually using the space on your Mac, where the big files usually hide, and how to clear them out without breaking anything.
1. See how much space you have
Open System Settings → General → Storage. The bar at the top shows how full your startup disk is, split into categories such as Applications, Documents, Photos, iOS Files and System Data.
Below the bar, macOS offers a few recommendations worth a look:
Store in iCloud keeps full-size photos and documents in iCloud and only recent ones on the Mac.
Optimize Storage removes Apple TV movies and shows you've already watched.
Empty Trash Automatically deletes items that have been in the Trash for 30 days.
What the Storage screen doesn't tell you is which folders are big. "Documents: 180 GB" could be one forgotten video project or a thousand small files.
2. Find what's actually using it

Finder can show folder sizes — in a list view, choose View → Show View Options and turn on Calculate all sizes — but you have to open every folder one by one, and it skips the parts of the disk Finder hides.
A disk space analyzer scans the whole disk at once and shows every folder by size. DiskGarden is a free one for the Mac:
Open DiskGarden and click your startup disk (usually "Macintosh HD"). A full scan takes seconds to a couple of minutes.
The disk appears as a bloom: each ring is a level of folders, and each petal is as wide as the space it takes. The widest petals are your biggest folders.
Hover a petal to see its name and size, click to grow into it, and keep going until you find the files that matter.
Drag what you don't need into the Waste bin. Nothing is deleted until you review the pile and empty it — and by default it goes to the Trash first.
If the total doesn't add up to what macOS reports, part of the disk is off limits to normal apps. A Deep Scan (Admin) maps it too.
3. Where the space usually goes
On most Macs a handful of places account for most of the space. Check these first:
Downloads and old installers
⟦0⟧ quietly collects disk images (.dmg), zip files and installers you only needed once. Sort by size and clear out what you've already installed.
iPhone and iPad backups

Local device backups can take tens of gigabytes each. With a device connected, select it in Finder's sidebar and click Manage Backups; or look directly in ⟦0⟧. Delete backups of devices you no longer own.
Developer files
Xcode DerivedData (⟦0⟧) is build output; it's safe to delete and rebuilds when needed.
iOS DeviceSupport (⟦0⟧) keeps symbols for every iOS version you've ever connected; old versions can go.
Simulators: ⟦0⟧ removes simulators for runtimes you no longer have.
Docker stores everything in one large disk image. Use ⟦0⟧, or lower the disk limit in Docker Desktop's settings.
Package caches: ⟦0⟧ for Homebrew, and the caches in ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ can be cleared and re-downloaded.
Caches
⟦0⟧ holds data apps can re-create, like browser caches and app updates. Quit the app first, then delete its cache folder. Expect it to grow back somewhat as you use the app.
Photos, videos and music

A Photos library or a folder of screen recordings and exported videos is often the single biggest item. With iCloud Photos, turn on Optimize Mac Storage in Photos settings to keep smaller versions on the Mac.
Mail attachments
Attachments you've opened are kept in ⟦0⟧.
Apps you no longer use
Large apps and their support files — GarageBand's and Logic's sound libraries, games, old Xcode versions — are easy to spot in the Applications folder and in ⟦0⟧.
4. Delete safely
Don't touch system folders. ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ and ⟦3⟧ belong to macOS. DiskGarden shows them so you understand your disk, but won't let you put them in the Waste bin.
Prefer the Trash. Moving files to the Trash gives you a way back. Empty it once you're sure.
Keep a backup of anything irreplaceable before a big cleanup.
5. Freed space not showing up?
macOS doesn't always hand space back immediately:
Files in the Trash still take space until you empty it.
Time Machine local snapshots can keep deleted files on disk for a while. macOS removes them when it needs the space; see System Data.
Some space is purgeable: macOS counts it as used, but frees it automatically when an app needs it. DiskGarden shows this as Available (incl. purgeable).
A restart often settles the numbers.

What is "System Data" on a Mac — and how do you shrink it?
In System Settings → General → Storage, "System Data" is often one of the biggest bars, and macOS won't say what's in it. Here's what it contains, why it grows, and what you can safely do about it.
What System Data is

System Data (older versions of macOS called it "Other") is the catch-all category in the Storage overview: everything that isn't an app, a document, a photo or another category macOS recognizes. It typically includes:
Caches — from macOS, browsers and apps, in ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧.
Time Machine local snapshots — copies of recently changed files kept on the startup disk.
Virtual machine and container disks — Docker, Parallels, UTM and similar store whole disks as single large files.
Developer data — Xcode build products, simulators and device symbols.
App support files — databases, downloaded models, game assets and more in ⟦0⟧.
Logs and temporary files, and the files macOS uses for virtual memory and sleep in ⟦0⟧.
How to see what's inside
The Storage screen doesn't break System Data down, and much of it lives in folders Finder hides. A disk space analyzer shows it folder by folder:
Scan your startup disk with DiskGarden (free).
Look at Users → your name → Library: Caches, Application Support, Containers and Developer are where most user-side System Data sits.
Space that DiskGarden can't read without extra rights — other users' files, protected system folders, snapshots — shows up as a purple hidden space petal. A Deep Scan (Admin) maps it.
How to reduce it safely
Restart, then wait a little
macOS clears many temporary files and purgeable data on its own, especially after a restart. Check Storage again afterwards before deleting anything by hand.
macOS keeps local snapshots so you can restore recent files even when your backup disk isn't connected, and deletes them automatically when space runs low. To see them, open Terminal and run:
To remove one, run ⟦0⟧ followed by its date (for example ⟦1⟧). Only do this if you need the space right away.
Quit the app, then delete its folder in ⟦0⟧. Apps rebuild what they need, so this frees space but some of it comes back.
Developer and container files
Delete ⟦0⟧ and old versions in ⟦1⟧.
Run ⟦0⟧ to remove simulators for runtimes you no longer have.
Run ⟦0⟧, or lower Docker Desktop's disk limit.
Delete virtual machines you no longer use from inside their app.
App support data

Large folders in ⟦0⟧ usually belong to an app: an old game, a music library, downloaded AI models. Remove the content from inside the app when you can, or delete the folder if you've already removed the app.
What not to delete
Anything in ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧ or ⟦3⟧.
The virtual memory and sleep files in ⟦0⟧ — macOS manages them.
Folders in ⟦0⟧ you don't recognize: they often belong to drivers or system components.
DiskGarden refuses to put system locations in the Waste bin, so you can explore freely without breaking anything.
Why Does macOS Take Up So Much Space on My Mac?
Why the macOS category in Storage settings is so large — system volume, Recovery, swap, downloaded assets, updates — and what you can actually reclaim.
Why does macOS take up so much space on my Mac?
In Storage settings, the "macOS" bar alone can be tens of gigabytes — before you've installed anything. Here's what's in it, what's fixed, and what you can actually reclaim.
What counts as "macOS"
Open System Settings → General → Storage and hover the bar. The macOS category is the operating system itself plus the files it needs to run, update and recover:

The system volume. Since macOS Big Sur, the system lives on a separate, read-only, cryptographically sealed volume. Nothing on it can be removed — and you wouldn't want to: the seal is what lets your Mac check the system hasn't been tampered with.
Recovery and Preboot. Small hidden volumes that let your Mac start up and reinstall macOS when something goes wrong.
Swap and sleep files in ⟦0⟧. When apps need more memory than you have, macOS writes some of it to swap files; the sleep image holds memory while the Mac sleeps. Both shrink on their own.
Downloaded system assets — fonts, dictionaries, voices, language and machine-learning models (including Apple Intelligence) — kept in ⟦0⟧.
Software updates that have been downloaded but not installed yet.
Some of what people think of as "macOS" is actually counted as System Data instead: caches, logs and Time Machine snapshots.
What you can reclaim
Install (or clear) a pending update
A downloaded macOS update can take several gigabytes until it's installed. Install it from System Settings → General → Software Update; afterwards the download is removed.
Restart to shrink swap
If you've had heavy apps open for days, swap files may have grown to many gigabytes. Quitting memory-hungry apps or restarting your Mac lets macOS remove them.
Remove downloaded voices and features you don't use
Extra Siri and spoken-content voices: System Settings → Accessibility → Spoken Content → System voice → Manage Voices…
Apple Intelligence's on-device models, if you don't use it: see How much storage Apple Intelligence uses.
Leave the rest alone
The sealed system volume, Recovery and Preboot can't (and shouldn't) be trimmed by hand. "Cleaner" apps that promise to shrink macOS itself mostly delete caches that come straight back.
See it for yourself

Storage settings only gives you totals. DiskGarden scans your startup disk and shows every folder by size — including ⟦0⟧, which it shows as a single block sized from the volume's real usage. Space the scan can't read appears as a purple hidden space petal; a Deep Scan (Admin) maps it.
How to Find Large Files on a Mac (3 Ways)
Three ways to find the biggest files and folders on your Mac: Storage settings, a Finder size search, and a disk space map that shows every folder at once.
How to find large files on a Mac
When your disk fills up, a handful of big files and folders are usually to blame. Here are three ways to find them — from built-in tools to a map of the whole disk.
1. Storage settings: "Large Files"

Open System Settings → General → Storage, then click the ⓘ button next to Documents. The Large Files tab lists big individual files in your home folder, sorted by size, and you can delete them from there.
It's quick, but limited: it lists files, not folders, so a folder of ten thousand 1 MB files never shows up — and it skips app data, caches and system locations.
2. A Finder size search
Open a Finder window and press ⌘ F. Choose This Mac as the search scope.
Click the first pop-up menu (usually Kind) and choose Other…, then tick File Size in the list.
Set the rule to is greater than 1 GB (or 500 MB).

Click Save to keep it as a Smart Folder in the sidebar. Like Storage settings, it finds big single files but not big folders, and Spotlight doesn't index everything (system folders and some app data are excluded).
3. A map of every folder
A disk space analyzer reads the whole disk and shows every folder with its total size — so a folder full of small files is as visible as one huge video. DiskGarden draws it as a bloom:
Open DiskGarden and click your startup disk. The scan takes seconds to a couple of minutes.
The widest petals are the biggest folders. Hover for the exact size; click to grow into a folder and follow the widest petals down to what's big.
Press Space to Quick Look a file, or right-click → Show in Finder.
Drag what you don't need into the Waste bin and empty it when you're sure — by default the files go to the Trash first.
What you'll usually find
Videos, screen recordings and exported projects.
Old iPhone and iPad backups.
Developer data: Xcode and Docker.
Disk images and installers in Downloads.
App caches and support data — see which caches are safe to delete.
Xcode Taking Up Space? Clean DerivedData and Simulators
Where Xcode's gigabytes go — DerivedData, simulator runtimes, device support, archives — and how to clean each one safely on your Mac.
Xcode taking up space? How to clean it up

Xcode is one of the biggest space users on a developer's Mac: build products, simulators, device symbols and archives can add up to well over 50 GB. Here's what each one is and how to clean it safely.
DerivedData: build products
⟦0⟧ holds intermediate build files and indexes for every project you've opened. It's safe to delete entirely — Xcode rebuilds what it needs the next time you build (the first build is slower).
Quit Xcode first, then delete the folder's contents, or delete just the folders of projects you no longer work on.
Simulator runtimes and devices

Runtimes (each iOS, watchOS, tvOS or visionOS version you've downloaded) can be several gigabytes each. Remove old ones in Xcode → Settings → Components (called Platforms in some versions), or list and delete them in Terminal with ⟦0⟧ and ⟦1⟧ followed by the runtime's identifier.
Simulator devices live in ⟦0⟧. ⟦1⟧ removes devices whose runtime is gone.
Simulator caches in ⟦0⟧ can be deleted; they're rebuilt as needed.
Device support files

Every time you connect a device running a new OS version, Xcode copies its debug symbols to ⟦0⟧ (and watchOS DeviceSupport, etc.). Each version takes a few gigabytes. Delete folders for versions you no longer debug on; Xcode copies them again if you reconnect such a device.
Archives

⟦0⟧ holds every app you've archived for distribution. Keep the archives of builds you've shipped (you need their debug symbols to read crash reports); older internal builds can go. Manage them in Window → Organizer.
Find out where your Xcode space went
DiskGarden shows ⟦0⟧ folder by folder, so you can see at a glance whether simulators, DerivedData or device support is the big one — then drag it into the Waste bin to remove it.
Using other toolchains too? Package caches add up as well: see which caches are safe to delete.
Docker Taking Up Space on Mac? Shrink Docker.raw Safely

Docker taking up space on your Mac? Here's how to shrink it
Docker Desktop keeps all images, containers, volumes and build cache inside one big disk image. It grows quietly — here's how to see what it really uses and get space back.
Where Docker's space goes
On a Mac, Docker runs Linux in a lightweight virtual machine. Everything inside it lives in one file, usually ⟦0⟧.

It's a sparse file: Finder may show its maximum size (for example 64 GB) while it actually uses much less. To see the real size, run ⟦0⟧ on it in Terminal — or scan with DiskGarden, which counts the space a file really occupies on disk.
See what's using it
Run ⟦0⟧ to see how much is taken by images, containers, local volumes and build cache, and how much of each is reclaimable.
Reclaim space
⟦0⟧ removes stopped containers, unused networks, dangling images and unused build cache.
⟦0⟧ also removes every image not used by a container — you'll re-download them when needed.
⟦0⟧ clears just the build cache, often the biggest part for people who build images often.
⟦0⟧ removes unused volumes. Careful: volumes hold data such as local databases; make sure you don't need it.
Docker Desktop hands freed space back to macOS automatically, though it can take a little while for the file to shrink.
Cap how big it can get
In Docker Desktop, open Settings → Resources and lower the virtual disk limit. Docker won't grow past it (lowering it may require resetting Docker's data, so prune first).
As a last resort, Troubleshoot → Clean / Purge data deletes everything Docker stores and starts fresh.
Other virtual machines

Parallels, UTM, VMware Fusion and similar apps also keep each virtual machine as one large file or bundle. Delete VMs you no longer use from inside the app. All of these show up in macOS's System Data.
How to Delete Old iPhone and iPad Backups on a Mac
Find and delete old iPhone and iPad backups stored on your Mac — in Finder or directly in the MobileSync folder — and what to keep before you do.
How to delete old iPhone and iPad backups on a Mac
Every local backup of an iPhone or iPad is a full copy of the device's data — often tens of gigabytes. Backups of phones you sold years ago can still be sitting on your Mac.
Delete backups in Finder
Connect an iPhone or iPad and select it in the Finder sidebar.
In the General tab, click Manage Backups…. You'll see every device backup on this Mac with its date.
Select an old backup, click Delete Backup, and confirm.
Backups marked with a lock are encrypted; they include saved passwords and Health data.
Or find them directly

Backups are stored in ⟦0⟧, one folder per backup with a long identifier as its name. In Finder, choose Go → Go to Folder… and paste that path. macOS protects this folder, so apps (including Terminal and DiskGarden) need Full Disk Access to see inside it.
With Full Disk Access, DiskGarden shows each backup folder with its size, so the big ones stand out.
What to keep
Keep the most recent backup of each device you still use — or make sure the device backs up to iCloud instead (iCloud backups don't use space on your Mac).
Before deleting the only backup of an old device, check you don't need anything from it (photos, messages).
Time Machine Local Snapshots Taking Up Space? What to Do
What Time Machine local snapshots are, why they use space on your Mac's disk, how to list them and when (and how) to delete them.
Time Machine local snapshots taking up space? What to do
If you use Time Machine, your Mac also keeps snapshots on its own disk. They're useful, they're temporary — and they're one reason freed space doesn't show up right away.
What local snapshots are

With Time Machine turned on, macOS takes a snapshot of your startup disk about every hour and keeps it for roughly a day. If your backup disk isn't connected, you can still restore a file you changed or deleted a few hours ago.

A snapshot keeps old versions of changed and deleted files. That's why deleting a large file sometimes doesn't free space at once: the snapshot still holds it until the snapshot expires. Snapshots count as purgeable space and show up in System Data.

Each line is one snapshot, named with its date and time (for example ⟦0⟧).
Delete them (only if you need the space now)

macOS deletes local snapshots automatically when disk space runs low, so usually you don't need to do anything. If you need the space right away — say, for a large install — delete a snapshot by its date:
You'll lose the ability to restore from that snapshot, but your Time Machine backups on the backup disk are unaffected.
How they look in DiskGarden

Snapshot space isn't part of any folder, so a normal scan can't attribute it. DiskGarden shows it as part of the purple hidden space petal, and the Available (incl. purgeable) figure tells you how much macOS can reclaim on its own.
What Is Purgeable Space on Mac — and How to Free It
Why your Mac shows purgeable space, why apps still say the disk is full, and how to turn purgeable space into free space.
What is purgeable space on a Mac — and how do you free it?
Finder says you have plenty of space, but an installer says the disk is full. The difference is purgeable space: storage macOS counts as available but hasn't actually freed yet.
What purgeable space is
Purgeable space is data macOS can delete on its own whenever something needs room:
iCloud Drive files that are safely in iCloud (with Optimize Mac Storage on), which macOS can remove locally and download again when you open them.
Time Machine local snapshots.
Some caches, and media you've already watched (with Optimize Storage).
Why the numbers don't agree

Finder's Get Info on your disk and Storage settings include purgeable space in "available". But some apps — and the ⟦0⟧ command — only count space that's actually free right now. An installer that checks free space may refuse to run even though Finder shows enough.
DiskGarden shows both: Available (really free now) and Available (incl. purgeable) (what macOS can free up).
How to turn it into free space
macOS frees purgeable space when an app asks for it, so most of the time you don't need to do anything. If an app won't start or install because it checks free space directly:
Restart your Mac; macOS tidies temporary and purgeable data during startup.
Delete local snapshots you don't need (see the snapshot guide).
Free real space by removing big files you don't need — here's how to find them.
Is Spotlight Taking Up Space on Your Mac? Check and Rebuild
How big the Spotlight index on your Mac is, why it sometimes balloons, and how to rebuild it or exclude folders.
Spotlight's index
Is Spotlight taking up space on your Mac? How to check and rebuild it
Spotlight keeps an index of your files so search is instant. Usually it's a few gigabytes; occasionally it grows far larger. Here's how to check, rebuild or shrink it.
Where the index lives

Each indexed volume has a hidden ⟦0⟧ folder at its top level. On your startup disk it's at ⟦1⟧; external drives have their own. The folder is protected, so you'll only see its size with administrator rights — in DiskGarden, run a Deep Scan (Admin).
An index of a few gigabytes is normal for a full disk. Much more than that, or an index that keeps growing, can mean it's damaged.
Check indexing status
In Terminal, ⟦0⟧ shows whether indexing is on for your startup disk. While Spotlight is (re)indexing, you'll see the ⟦1⟧ and ⟦2⟧ processes busy in Activity Monitor.
Rebuild the index
If search misbehaves or the index looks far too big, erase and rebuild it:
Spotlight rebuilds the index in the background; search results are incomplete for a while (from minutes to a few hours on a big disk).
Keep folders out of the index

Folders with huge numbers of files you never search — build output, package caches, VM images — make the index bigger for no benefit. Add them to Spotlight's Search Privacy list in System Settings → Spotlight.

How Much Storage Does Apple Intelligence Use on a Mac?
How much disk space Apple Intelligence's on-device models need on a Mac, where it shows up in Storage settings, and how to get it back if you don't use it.
How much storage does Apple Intelligence use on a Mac?
Apple Intelligence runs its models on your Mac, and those models are downloaded to your disk. Here's roughly how much space that takes, where it shows up, and how to get it back if you don't use it.
How much space it needs

Apple says Apple Intelligence needs about 7 GB of available storage on a Mac, and the requirement has grown as features were added. The models download in the background after you turn it on, so the space goes quietly.
Other on-device features — Siri voices, dictation and translation languages — download their own assets too.
Where it shows up

The models are system assets, so in System Settings → General → Storage they count toward macOS (or System Data), not toward any app. They're stored in protected system locations, so you can't — and shouldn't — delete them by hand.
Getting the space back

If you don't use Apple Intelligence, turn it off in System Settings → Apple Intelligence & Siri. macOS can then remove the downloaded models; the space may take a while to come back. Turning it on again downloads them again.
To see how your disk's space is split overall, scan your startup disk with DiskGarden — and if the macOS category is still large, see why macOS takes up so much space.
Do You Need a Mac Cleaner App? What Actually Frees Space
What Mac cleaner apps really remove, why the space comes back, and what frees more disk space for good: finding the large files you don't need.
Do you need a Mac cleaner app?
Cleaner apps promise a faster Mac and gigabytes of free space at the press of a button. Here's what they actually remove, why the space often comes back, and what works better when your disk is full.
What cleaner apps remove
Most "one-click" cleaners delete the same kinds of files: app and browser caches, logs, temporary files, language files inside apps, and leftover files from removed apps.
macOS already manages most of these. It clears temporary files on its own, rotates logs, and removes purgeable data when space runs low.
Why the space comes back

Caches exist to make apps faster. Delete them and apps rebuild them as you use them — so the space you "freed" slowly returns, and apps can feel slower in the meantime. That's why a cleaner can report gigabytes freed every week.
Some cleaners also remove things you may want: app language files break features in some apps, and deleting files in ⟦0⟧ blindly can reset an app's settings or data.
What actually frees space

On almost every full Mac, a few large items take most of the space: videos and projects, old iPhone backups, Xcode or Docker data, disk images in Downloads, a photo library. Removing one of them usually frees more than a cleaner ever will — and it stays freed.

The hard part is finding them. A disk space analyzer like DiskGarden shows every folder by size, so the big ones stand out in seconds. You decide what goes, review it in the Waste bin, and system files can't be removed by accident.
When cleaning caches does help
An app misbehaves and its support page says to clear its cache.
A developer cache (Homebrew, npm, Gradle, DerivedData) has grown to many gigabytes — see which caches are safe to delete.
You need a little space right now, for an update or an install.
Is It Safe to Delete Caches on a Mac? Which Ones and How
Which Mac caches are safe to delete (user caches, browser caches, package managers), which to leave alone, and how much space they really free.
Is it safe to delete caches on a Mac? Which ones, and how
Caches are files apps keep to work faster, and they're the first thing "cleaner" apps delete. Some are safe to clear, some aren't worth it, and a few you shouldn't touch.
Usually safe to delete
Your user caches in ⟦0⟧. Quit the app first, then delete its folder. The app rebuilds what it needs.

Browser caches: clear them from the browser's own settings (for example Safari → Settings → Advanced → Show features for web developers, then Develop → Empty Caches; or Chrome → Delete browsing data → Cached images and files).
Developer and package caches: ⟦0⟧, ⟦1⟧, ⟦2⟧, ⟦3⟧, ⟦4⟧, and Xcode's DerivedData. They re-download or rebuild on demand.
Be careful with
⟦0⟧: shared by all users and some system components. Usually safe, but there's little to gain.
Folders in ⟦0⟧: these aren't caches — they hold app data such as libraries, saved games and settings. Only delete a folder there if you've already removed the app.
Don't touch
⟦0⟧ and anything else under ⟦1⟧ belongs to macOS (most of it is protected anyway). DiskGarden won't let you put system locations in the Waste bin.
How much will you get back?

Often a few gigabytes — and some of it comes back as you use your apps. Caches are rarely the main reason a Mac runs out of space; it's usually a few big folders. Scan with DiskGarden to see whether ⟦0⟧ is actually big on your Mac before deleting anything, and find the large files that matter more.
